shared.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
shared.description:
Aboriginal Peoples are the Traditional custodians of Australia and are represented by more than 250 language groups, each connected with a particular Country. Torres Strait Islander Peoples are represented by 5 major island groups and are connected with islands to the north of Australia’s Cape York which were annexed by Queensland in 1879. 

An Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander person is someone who: 

  • is of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander descent 
  • identifies as an Aboriginal person and/or Torres Strait Islander person, and 
  • is accepted as such by the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Community(ies) in which they live.

shared.title: Aboriginal English
shared.description: A recognised dialect of English which is the first, or home language, of many Aboriginal people. It differs from other dialects of English, such as Standard Australian English, in systematic ways including sounds, grammar, words and their meanings, and language use. Aboriginal English is a powerful vehicle for the expression of Aboriginal identity. Aboriginal English is not a target language study option for NSW Aboriginal Languages syllabuses.

shared.title: Aboriginal Songline(s)
shared.description: Texts that describe landscapes and directions of the tracks forged in lands, waters and skies by Creator Spirits during the Dreaming.

shared.title: accessibility
shared.description: The extent to which a system, environment or object may be used irrespective of a user’s capabilities or abilities. For example, the use of assistive technologies (AT) to allow people with disability to use computer systems, or the use of icons in place of words to allow young children to use a system.

shared.title: assistive technology (AT)
shared.description: A device or system whose primary purpose is to maintain or improve an individual's functioning and independence to facilitate participation and enhance overall wellbeing. This includes technologies specifically designed to meet an individual's needs, eg eye gaze technology, as well as more general technologies that can be used by anyone, eg speech-to-text applications. Assistive technology can also be referred to as inclusive technology.

shared.title: augmentative and alternative communication (AAC)
shared.description:
An umbrella term that encompasses the communication methods used to supplement or replace speech or writing. AAC can be unaided, such as gestures, body language and sign language, or aided such as pictures, symbols, objects or speech generating devices.

See communication systems

shared.title: communication forms
shared.description: The ways people communicate and the communicative behaviours they use. Communication forms can be non-symbolic and/or symbolic. Non-symbolic forms include sounds, gestures, facial expressions and eye movements. Symbolic forms can be aided or non-aided. Aided forms of symbolic communication include objects, symbols, photographs and drawings. Aided forms can be digital. Non-aided forms of symbolic communication include formal gestures; speech; and signs, such as Key Word Sign.

shared.title: copyright
shared.description: The protection provided to the creators of original works and makers of sound recordings and films, that offers a legal framework for the control and reproduction or transmission of their literary, dramatic, artistic or musical works.

shared.title: Country/Place
shared.description:
Country is used to describe a specific area of a nation or clan including physical, linguistic and spiritual features. Aboriginal communities’ cultural associations with their Country may include or relate to languages, cultural practices, knowledge, songs, stories, art, paths, landforms, flora, fauna and minerals. These cultural associations may include custodial relationships with particular landscapes such as land, sea, sky, rivers as well as the intangible places associated with the Dreaming(s). Custodial relationships are extremely important in determining who may have the capacity to authentically speak for their Country. 

Place is a space mapped out by physical or intangible boundaries that individuals or groups of Torres Strait Islander Peoples occupy and regard as their own. It is a space with varying degrees of spirituality.

shared.title: culture
shared.description: The customs, habits, beliefs/spirituality, social organisation and ways of life that characterise different groups and communities. Cultural characteristics give a group or individual a sense of who they are and help them make sense of the world in which they live. Culture is a shared system but inherently diverse – there can be individual and group differences within cultures. Everyone has culture – it is a lens through which we see the world.

shared.title: custodians
shared.description: In Aboriginal communities, an individual charged with maintaining and passing on particular elements of cultural significance, eg language, stories, songs, rituals and imagery.

shared.title: d/Deaf
shared.description: When referring to deaf people who belong to a linguistic and cultural minority known as the Deaf community, the 'D' may be capitalised in reference to the individual, the group, or the culture in order to accord respect and deference, for example, the Deaf community. When referring simply to audiological status or when cultural affiliation is not known, as in the case of a person with a hearing loss in general, the lowercase 'd', as in 'deaf' is the more common usage.

shared.title: Deaf
shared.description: A cultural identity for people with hearing loss who share a common culture and who usually have a shared sign language.

shared.title: disability
shared.description:
An umbrella term for any or all of the following components: 

  • impairments: challenges in body function or structure
  • activity limitations: difficulties in executing activities
  • participation restrictions: challenges an individual may experience in involvement in life situations. (World Health Organization)

shared.title: diversity
shared.description: Differences that exist within a group, for example, age, sex, gender, gender expression, sexuality, ethnicity, ability/disability, body shape and composition, culture, religion/spirituality, learning differences, socioeconomic background, values and experiences.

shared.title: Dreaming
shared.description: The Dreaming has different meanings for different Aboriginal groups. The Dreaming can be seen as the embodiment of Aboriginal creation which gives meaning to everything; the essence of Aboriginal beliefs about creation and spiritual and physical existence. It establishes the rules governing relationships between the people, the land and all things for Aboriginal Peoples. The Dreaming is linked to the past, the present and the future. Where appropriate, refer to Aboriginal names for the Dreaming.

shared.title: Elders
shared.description: The custodians of knowledge and lore. They are chosen and accepted by their own communities as people who have the permission to disclose cultural knowledge and beliefs. Recognised Elders are highly respected people within Aboriginal communities. Proper consultation with local Aboriginal communities will often direct schools to recognised Elders.

shared.title: first language(s)
shared.description: The first language(s) that a person learns to speak.

shared.title: Indigenous
shared.description:
An internationally recognised term for the first peoples of a land. In NSW the term Aboriginal person/Peoples is preferred.

See Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

shared.title: Indigenous cultural and intellectual property (ICIP)
shared.description:
Includes, but is not limited to, objects, sites, cultural knowledge, cultural expression and the arts, that have been transmitted or continue to be transmitted through generations as belonging to a particular Indigenous group or Indigenous people as a whole or their territory. 

See intellectual property

shared.title: intellectual property
shared.description:
Non-material assets such as forms of cultural expression that belong to a particular individual or community. Intellectual property rights refer to the rights that the law grants to individuals for the protection of creative, intellectual, scientific and industrial activity, such as inventions. 

See Indigenous cultural and intellectual property (ICIP), and copyright

shared.title: Key Word Sign
shared.description: A communication strategy that incorporates signing with speech. It is used to support language development for people with communication difficulties. Although Key Word Sign uses a simplified form of manual signing, it is different to Auslan, as it is not a signed language.

shared.title: kinship
shared.description: A key aspect of Aboriginal cultures and values. It includes the importance of all relationships and of being related to and belonging to the land.

shared.title: language group
shared.description: An Aboriginal community identified with a common language, both verbal and nonverbal, and with a particular territory. Used in preference to the term ‘tribe’.

shared.title: language revival
shared.description: The process and range of strategies for increasing knowledge and use of a language that is no longer spoken fluently across all generations in the context of language loss or language dispossession caused by colonisation. Aboriginal Languages and Torres Strait Islander Languages are being revived through community initiatives, linguistic research and school programs. ‘Language revival’ may be used as an overarching term that could also include ‘reclamation’, ‘revitalisation’, ‘renewal’ and ‘reawakening’.

shared.title: local Aboriginal community
shared.description:
A local Aboriginal community is constituted by those people who are Aboriginal and who reside in the near locality. Aboriginal communities will have a rich and diverse history that has been seriously affected by dispossession and relations, which sees families with spiritual connection to Country residing beside those who have been forced to move from other locations. The notion of locality is complex and multilayered: schools should seek advice from a range of people and/or organisations representing local interests. 

See community(ies)

shared.title: off-Country
shared.description:
Taking place away from Aboriginal land or Country of origin. 

See Country/Place

shared.title: on-Country
shared.description:
Taking place on Aboriginal land or Country of origin.

See Country/Place

shared.title: protocols
shared.description: The appropriate ways of behaving, communicating and showing respect for diversity of history and culture. This involves appreciation of the knowledge, standing and status of people within the local Aboriginal community and the school community. Protocols inevitably vary between communities, and between people within a community. In establishing a partnership between schools and Aboriginal communities, it is especially important that protocols are acknowledged and respected.

shared.title: sign
shared.description: Hand signs (or hand talk) used to supplement or replace oral language. Signs form part of nonverbal communication for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and may be used by people who are hearing, or d/Deaf or hard of hearing. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages may be used in some areas. Some Sign Languages may be associated with sacred ceremonial practices.

shared.title: signage
shared.description: The use of words, graphic designs and/or symbols used to communicate a message, eg information signs, plaques, warning signs, road signs, signs that show direction.

shared.title: switch
shared.description:
A type of assistive technology that enables people with cognitive and/or physical disability to access a range of devices, including computers and communication devices. Switches can be activated by touch, or triggered without contact, such as through eye gaze, sound or blowing.

See assistive technology (AT)

shared.title: yarning circle
shared.description: Yarning circles are an important cultural practice for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to learn within the collective group. Knowledge and information are shared in harmony and respect with all individuals.

specific.title: access content points
specific.description: Content for students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards the Early Stage 1 outcomes. Teachers can use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome.

specific.title: adjectival clause
specific.description: A type of dependent clause that operates as an adjective to give more information to a noun or pronoun in a sentence.

specific.title: adjectival phrase
specific.description:
A group of words (usually beginning with a preposition) that gives more information about a noun.

For example:

  • The girl with brown curly hair sat at the front.
  • The flowers in the vase were wilting.

specific.title: adjective
specific.description: A word class that describes, classifies or qualifies a noun or a pronoun.

specific.title: adverb
specific.description: A word that tells something about a verb, adjective, another adverb or a whole clause. They usually indicate manner (commonly ending in -ly) or degree.

specific.title: adverbial clause
specific.description: A dependent clause that modifies a verb, adjective, adverb or a main clause in a sentence.

specific.title: adverbial phrase
specific.description:
A group of words that provides information about where, when, with what, how far, how long, with whom, about what or as what.

For example:

  • He swept the floor with an old broom.
  • Throughout time people have attempted to halt old age.

specific.title: aesthetic
specific.description: Relating to a sense of beauty or an appreciation of artistic expression.

specific.title: analyse
specific.description: Identify components and the relationship between them; draw out and relate implications.

specific.title: anaphor(a)
specific.description:
Grammar – a word or phrase that references an earlier word or phrase.

Rhetoric – the intentional repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of several clauses, sentences, stanzas or paragraphs.

specific.title: antonym
specific.description: A word or phrase that has the opposite meaning of another word or phrase.

specific.title: apostrophe (’)
specific.description: A punctuation marker used to indicate possession or missing letters or numbers in a contracted expression.

specific.title: appositive
specific.description:
A noun or pronoun that is positioned beside another noun or pronoun to explain or identify it. An appositive often includes modifiers.

See modifier

specific.title: appreciate
specific.description: Make a judgement about the value of.

specific.title: appropriation
specific.description: Taking a text or component of a text (such as a character or plot) from one context and using it in another context.

specific.title: argument
specific.description:
A stated position about an idea.

The way in which various dimensions of a text (such as theme, perspective and style) can be understood to represent a particular position on an issue.

specific.title: assess
specific.description: Make a judgement of value, quality, outcomes, results or size.

specific.title: assimilated prefix
specific.description: A bound morpheme that is added before a base word and where its last letter changes to match the first letter of the base word. For example, in + mature = immature.

specific.title: audience
specific.description: Readers, listeners or viewers who engage with a text.

specific.title: authority
specific.description:
Authority of a text – How trustworthy, authentic or valid an audience may find the representation of ideas, experiences, perspectives and arguments in a text.

Authority over a text – The varying degrees to which the meaning of a text is controlled or constructed by its creator(s) and by its audience.

specific.title: authorship
specific.description: Origin as to author, composer, or compiler. For example, the authorship of a book.

specific.title: automaticity
specific.description: The fast, accurate and effortless word recognition that comes with practice. NESA acknowledges that reading aloud may include the use of Auslan, assistive technology or AACs.

specific.title: background knowledge
specific.description: Information that is important for understanding a subject.

specific.title: base word
specific.description:
A morpheme (meaningful unit) that stands freely on its own to make a word.

See morpheme

specific.title: blend
specific.description: The act of synthesising phonemes smoothly from left to right, to read words.

specific.title: causal connective
specific.description: A word or groups of words used as a cohesive device between sentences, when explaining how something works or why something happens.

specific.title: character
specific.description: A person (or animal) created in a text (usually narrative) to represent human characteristics including physical, emotional and intellectual characteristics, habits and behaviour.

specific.title: characterisation
specific.description: The technical construction and representation of any personality or person-like figure in text, including features such as their appearance, actions, words or thoughts.

specific.title: clarify
specific.description: Make clear or plain.

specific.title: clause (dependent)
specific.description: A dependent clause (also known as subordinate clause) is a group of words that cannot stand alone as a sentence.

specific.title: clause (main)
specific.description:
A main clause (also known as principal or independent clause) is a clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence.

See adjectival clause and adverbial clause

specific.title: code and convention
specific.description: Agreed systems of making, communicating and interpreting meaning.

specific.title: cohesive devices
specific.description: Words or phrases that indicate a relationship with other words, phrases, clauses or paragraphs across a text.

specific.title: comma (,)
specific.description: A punctuation marker used to show separation between parts of a sentence, such as clauses or phrases, where separation is important to the meaning. Commas are also used to separate words, phrases or numbers in a series.

specific.title: communication systems
specific.description: The range of communication forms used by a person. Communication systems are specifically designed to meet people’s individual needs.

specific.title: compare
specific.description: Show how things are similar or different.

specific.title: complex sentence
specific.description: Formed by adding one or more dependent (subordinate) clauses to a main (independent) clause using subordinating conjunctions and/or relative pronouns.

specific.title: compose
specific.description:
Develop and/or produce signed, spoken, written or multimodal texts in print, visual, oral or digital forms.

See create

specific.title: compound sentence
specific.description: A sentence comprising 2 or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.

specific.title: compound word
specific.description: A word consisting of 2 or more base words, e.g. farmyard = farm + yard.

specific.title: conditional connective
specific.description: A word, or groups of words, that describes the condition that needs to be met for something to happen. This may be in the form of a word ‘if’ or phrase ‘in this case’.

specific.title: conjunction
specific.description: A form of connective. A word or group of words used to link together words, phrases or clauses within sentences.

specific.title: connective
specific.description: A word or group of words used to connect sentences, clauses, phrases or words. A connective is commonly a conjunction, a preposition or an adverb.

specific.title: connotation
specific.description: The nuances or implied meaning attached to language, beyond that of its literal or dictionary meanings. Connotations may be positive, negative, or neutral.

specific.title: consonant digraph
specific.description:
Two consonant graphemes used to represent one phoneme.

For example:

  • th in that
  • sh in shy
  • kn in knee.

specific.title: consonant phoneme
specific.description: A speech sound produced with a complete or partial obstruction of the flow of air by the teeth, lips, tongue and/or voice.

specific.title: construct
specific.description: Make; build; put together items or arguments.

specific.title: context
specific.description: The range of personal, situational, social, historical and cultural circumstances that shape how texts and their representations are conceived, constructed, understood and interpreted.

specific.title: contraction
specific.description: A shortened form of one or 2 words (one of which is usually a verb). In a contraction, an apostrophe takes the place of the missing letter or letters.

specific.title: contrast
specific.description: Show how things are different or opposite.

specific.title: conventions
specific.description: Accepted practices or features that help define textual forms, creative forms, styles and meaning.

specific.title: coordinating conjunction
specific.description:
A word or group of words that functions to link:

  • 2 words or phrases within a sentence, e.g. shoes and socks
  • 2 independent clauses within a sentence.

specific.title: create
specific.description:
Develop and/or produce signed, spoken, written or multimodal texts in print, visual, oral or digital forms.

See compose

specific.title: CVC words
specific.description: Words formed by a consonant-vowel-consonant. For example, cat, bag, pen.

specific.title: dash
specific.description: A punctuation marker used to indicate an abrupt break or pause in a sentence, to begin and end a parenthetic clause, as an indication of omitted letters or words.

specific.title: declarative sentence
specific.description: A statement presented as a complete sentence to provide fact, evidence or detail. For example: Drinking water is important for your health.

specific.title: decodable texts
specific.description:
Texts that are made up of grapheme–phoneme correspondences (GPCs) that students have learnt. These texts are used by beginning readers to practise segmenting and blending skills to read words, quickly and effortlessly.

See automaticity

specific.title: decode
specific.description: A process of efficient word recognition in which readers use knowledge of the relationship between letters (graphemes) and sounds (phonemes) to work out how to say and read written words.

specific.title: define
specific.description: State meaning and identify essential qualities.

specific.title: definite article
specific.description: In English, the definite article is the word ‘the’. It’s located before a noun to indicate that the noun is specific.

specific.title: demonstrate
specific.description: Show by example.

specific.title: derivational word form
specific.description: A new word that is formed from another word, usually by adding a derivational suffix to change its grammatical form. For example, the noun, proposition, derives from the verb, propose, and contains the derivational suffix, -ion.

specific.title: describe
specific.description: Provide characteristics and features.

specific.title: dialogue
specific.description: A conversation between 2 or more people: the conversation between characters in a text, an exchange of ideas or opinions on a particular issue, or a literary work in the form of a conversation.

specific.title: digital text
specific.description: An audio, visual or multimodal text produced by electronic technology. A digital text may be interactive and include still and/or dynamic images, animations and/or hyperlinks.

specific.title: digraph
specific.description:
Two graphemes used to represent one phoneme.

For example:

  • consonant digraphs – sh, ck, th
  • split digraphs – a-e, i-e, o-e
  • vowel digraphs – ee, oo, ea.

specific.title: diphthong
specific.description: A type of vowel phoneme, also known as a glide vowel, formed by combining 2 vowel sounds within a single syllable. For example, /oi/ in join, /ou/ in proud.

specific.title: discursive text
specific.description: Texts whose primary focus is to explore an idea or variety of topics. These texts involve the discussion of an idea(s) or opinion(s) without the direct intention of persuading the reader, listener or viewer to adopt any single point of view.

specific.title: discuss
specific.description: Identify issues and provide points for and/or against.

specific.title: double consonant
specific.description: Two of the same consecutive letters. Also referred to as a consonant doublet.

specific.title: encode
specific.description: Spell words in their visible written form.

specific.title: etymology
specific.description:
The origins of, and changes to, words in relation to meaning.

Words derived from earlier or other languages, place names, words derived from people's names, coinages.

specific.title: evaluate
specific.description: Make a judgement based on criteria; determine the value of.

specific.title: examine
specific.description: Inquire into.

specific.title: exclamation mark
specific.description: A punctuation marker used after an exclamation.

specific.title: exclamatory sentence
specific.description: A statement expressing a strong emotion, formed as a complete sentence, and often ending with an exclamation mark.

specific.title: expanded noun group
specific.description: An extended group of words that provide rich or detailed information about the noun.

specific.title: expanded verb group
specific.description: A main verb that is preceded by one or more auxiliary or modal verbs to provide detail or precision.

specific.title: explain
specific.description: Relate cause and effect; make the relationships between things evident; or provide why and/or how.

specific.title: extended phonic code
specific.description: The vowel and consonant phonemes which are represented by less frequently occurring and alternative spellings.

specific.title: figurative language
specific.description: Word groups/phrases used differently from the expected or everyday usage to express an idea in a non-literal way for a particular effect.

specific.title: fluency
specific.description: Reading, speaking, encoding and spelling with appropriate pace and accuracy.

specific.title: fluent reading
specific.description: The act of identifying words accurately, effortlessly, at a contextually appropriate rate, and with phrasing and expression that reflects the meaning of the passage.

specific.title: full stop (.)
specific.description: A punctuation marker used to indicate the end of a sentence that is a statement or command.

specific.title: genre
specific.description:
The categories into which texts are grouped based on similarities in premise, structure and function. The ‘genre’ of a text describes larger recurring patterns of subject matter and textual structures observable between texts, such as typical plots, characters and setting.

‘Genre’ can also describe categories of form and structure in texts.

specific.title: gesture
specific.description: A nonverbal form of communication using movement of part of the body, such as a hand or the head, to express a message.

specific.title: gist statements
specific.description: Succinct thoughts and information that capture the generalisations gleaned from what has been read, heard or viewed.

specific.title: grammar
specific.description: A description of a language’s system, in regard to both structure (form) and meaning (function), at the level of a word, sentence and/or text.

specific.title: grapheme
specific.description:
The smallest unit of writing used to represent one phoneme. A letter or combination of letters corresponding to or representing a single phoneme.

Examples include:

  • the f in frog
  • the ph in phone
  • the gh in cough

specific.title: grapheme–phoneme correspondence
specific.description: The relationship between phoneme and its written alphabetic symbol (grapheme).

specific.title: high-frequency words
specific.description: Words that appear often in written texts.

specific.title: home language
specific.description: A language acquired and used in the home or community.

specific.title: homonym
specific.description: A word having the same sound and the same spelling as another, but a different meaning.

specific.title: homophone
specific.description: A word having the same sound as another but different spelling and meaning.

specific.title: hybrid text
specific.description: Composite texts resulting from combining elements from different genres, styles and modes.

specific.title: hyperbole
specific.description: An exaggerated statement not intended to be taken literally; may be used as a rhetorical device or figure of speech.

specific.title: hyperlink
specific.description: A hyperlink is a text, image, frame or button that when clicked or tapped will open another webpage, website, image, sound, document or application, such as email. Hyperlinks are often used within documents to link to other pages or sections.

specific.title: hyphen
specific.description: A punctuation marker used to connect the parts of a compound word or the parts of a word divided for any purpose.

specific.title: hyphenation
specific.description: Used at the end of a line, to break a word between syllables or morphemes.

specific.title: identify
specific.description: Recognise and name.

specific.title: idiom
specific.description: A commonly used phrase or expression, usually figurative or non-literal, that has an understood meaning specific to a language or dialect, e.g. over the moon, half asleep, pull your socks up.

specific.title: imagery
specific.description: Use of figurative language to represent objects, characters, actions or ideas in such a way that they appeal to the senses of the reader or viewer.

specific.title: imaginative text
specific.description: Texts that represent ideas, feelings and mental images in words or visual images. Imaginative texts entertain or provoke thought through their creative use of literary elements and make connections between ideas and experiences.

specific.title: imperative sentence
specific.description: A complete sentence conveying a direct command, request, invitation, warning or instruction, typically directed to an implied person.

specific.title: indefinite article
specific.description: In English, the indefinite article is either the word ‘a’ or ‘an’. It’s located before a noun to indicate that the noun is general.

specific.title: inference
specific.description: A conclusion reached on the basis of evidence and reasoning.

specific.title: inferencing
specific.description:
Local inferencing requires the reader to comprehend implied information from within relatively small sections of text, such as 2 adjacent sentences.

Global inferencing requires the reader to comprehend implied information from across relatively larger sections of text and is supported by the reader’s depth of vocabulary and background knowledge.

specific.title: inflected word forms
specific.description:
A word form that marks a distinction in tense (jump-jumps-jumping-jumped), plurality (cat-cats), and comparatives and superlatives (big-bigger-biggest).

See suffix

specific.title: informative text
specific.description: Texts whose primary purpose is to provide information through explanation, description, argument, analysis, ordering and presentation of evidence and procedures.

specific.title: interpersonal conventions
specific.description: Contextually purposeful language resources used for interacting; expressing ideas, opinions and feelings; and/or for taking a stance.

specific.title: interpret
specific.description: Draw meaning from.

specific.title: interrogative sentence
specific.description: A sentence that asks a direct or indirect question.

specific.title: intertextuality
specific.description: The various ways in which texts may be understood to draw meaning from one another, either by explicit, implied or inferred reference.

specific.title: intonation
specific.description: The pattern or melody of pitch changes in connected speech, especially the pitch pattern of a sentence.

specific.title: investigate
specific.description: Plan, inquire into and draw conclusions about.

specific.title: irregular plural word
specific.description:
A noun that indicates more than one thing without requiring a plural marking suffix, -s or -es.

Mouse is a singular noun and mice is an irregular noun.

specific.title: justify
specific.description: Support an argument or conclusion.

specific.title: lexical cohesion
specific.description: The use of word associations to create links in texts. Examples of links are the use of repetition of words, pronouns, synonyms, antonyms and words that are related, such as by class and subclass.

specific.title: literal
specific.description: Having only the most direct meaning.

specific.title: literary value
specific.description:
The many ways in which audiences across time assign importance to texts. This may include the perceived authenticity, universality or significance of their representations of personal, social or cultural experiences and ideas. It may also include the aesthetic qualities and artistic significance of a text.

Specific texts that are considered to hold enduring value for society are often termed ‘canonical’ or ‘classic’ texts.

specific.title: literature
specific.description: An evolving category of text that is broadly seen by its audience to hold enduring personal, social, cultural or aesthetic value. Literature comprises a dynamic range of fiction and nonfiction texts from diverse historical and cultural contexts.

specific.title: media
specific.description:
Means of communication, such as publishing, broadcasting or the internet.

Plural of medium.

specific.title: medium
specific.description:
Means of communication, such as publishing, broadcasting or the internet.

Singular of media.

specific.title: mental model
specific.description: A mental representation of the information in a real or an imaginary world. A student develops a mental model as the text progresses. It may include information derived from inferences and from background knowledge as well as from what is explicitly stated in the text itself.

specific.title: mentor text
specific.description: A text that is studied as an example to show how specific textual features are crafted. Also known as a model text.

specific.title: metalanguage
specific.description: Technical terms used to describe and discuss how language and texts function.

specific.title: metaphor
specific.description:
Linguistic – a figure of speech used for effect that implies one thing by referring to another.

Literary – an object, entity or situation that can be regarded as representing something else.

specific.title: modality
specific.description: Aspects of language that suggest a particular perspective on subjects and/or events. Modality forms a continuum from high modality (always, must) to low modality (might, could).

specific.title: mode
specific.description: A semiotic (meaning-making) resource or process of communication. For example, sounds, music, printed or spoken words, images and gestures.

specific.title: model text
specific.description: A text that is studied as an example to show how specific textual features are crafted. Also known as a mentor text.

specific.title: modifier
specific.description: Words, phrases and clauses that affect and often enhance the meaning of a sentence.

specific.title: monitoring
specific.description: Considering meaning and/or purpose when reading and/or writing.

specific.title: morpheme
specific.description: The smallest unit of meaning in a word, e.g. jumps has 2 morphemes: jump + s.

specific.title: morphological generalisation
specific.description: A spelling term that describes the manipulation and control of a particular base or root word when it is affixed with a prefix and/or suffix.

specific.title: multimodal text/presentation
specific.description: A text that combines 2 or more expressive modes to communicate.

specific.title: multisyllabic words
specific.description: Words of 2 or more syllables.

specific.title: narrative
specific.description: An account of events or experiences, which are real or imagined. In English literary theory, narrative includes a story (what is narrated) and a discourse (how it is narrated). Narrative can present as an explicit sequencing of events (type of text) or it can be an implied or inferred component in a text.

specific.title: navigation pathway
specific.description: A possible way to move around and locate content on a digital platform.

specific.title: nominalisation
specific.description: A process of transforming actions or events (verbs) or descriptions of nouns and pronouns (adjectives) into things, concepts or people (nouns). It can also refer to the process of forming noun groups from clauses. Nominalisation is often a feature of texts that contain abstract ideas and concepts.

specific.title: non-words
specific.description:
Words that contain phoneme–grapheme correspondences that are plausible.

Also referred to as pseudowords. For example, drot, shann, glick.

specific.title: nonfiction
specific.description: Text intended to convey the truth.

specific.title: noun
specific.description:
A word used to represent people, places, ideas and things.

  • Common nouns: nouns used to name any one of a class of things, e.g. girl, classroom, egg.
  • Proper nouns: nouns used to name a place, a person or the title of something and are signalled by a capital letter, e.g. Wagga Wagga, Sam, Olympic Games.
  • Collective nouns: nouns used to name a group of things, e.g. crowd, swarm, team.
  • Abstract nouns: nouns used to name things that we cannot see but which exist in thoughts and feelings, e.g. sadness, love, wonder.

See pronoun

specific.title: noun group
specific.description:
A group of words built around a noun.

Noun groups:

  • include a noun and any words that modify it
  • may include articles, adjectives and other modifiers
  • operate the same way as a single noun in the structure of a sentence.

specific.title: noun–pronoun agreement
specific.description: Occurs where the correct pronoun is selected for the noun or noun group to which it is referring. For example: The children were looking for their father in the supermarket.

specific.title: noun–verb agreement
specific.description:
Occurs where the correct verb is selected for the noun or noun group to which it is referring.

For example:

  • A singular subject has a singular verb: the apple is cold.
  • A plural subject has a plural verb: these apples are cold.

specific.title: object
specific.description: The noun, noun group or pronoun in a sentence that is affected by an action. For example: The child threw the ball.

specific.title: objective language
specific.description: Language that is fact-based, measurable and observable, verifiable and unbiased. It does not include a speaker or writer’s point of view, interpretation or judgement.

specific.title: onomatopoeia
specific.description: A word that phonetically imitates or is indicative of the sound that it describes. For example, bang, splash, oink, miaow.

specific.title: onset
specific.description:
The consonant speech sound(s) that appear at the start of a syllable and before the vowel phoneme. For example, /b/ represents the onset in the word ‘big’.

See rime

specific.title: oral language
specific.description: A system through which spoken words can be used to express, receive and understand information, ideas and feelings.

specific.title: orthography
specific.description: The conventional written or visible word-level system of a language.

specific.title: paragraph
specific.description: A sequence of sentences, grouped together and focused on a specific theme. A distinct section of writing indicated by a new line.

specific.title: paraphrase
specific.description: A rewording of something that has been written or spoken.

specific.title: parenthesis
specific.description:
A punctuation marker used to indicate an interjected explanatory or qualifying remark.

Plural: parentheses

specific.title: personification
specific.description:
Attributing human characteristics to abstractions such as love, things or animals.

See figurative language

specific.title: perspective
specific.description: A lens through which the author perceives the world and creates a text, or the lens through which the reader or viewer perceives the world and understands a text. Readers may also temporarily adopt the perspectives of others as a way of understanding texts.

specific.title: persuasive text
specific.description: A text designed to convince a reader of a particular opinion or way of thinking on an issue. A persuasive text may express an opinion while discussing, analysing and/or evaluating an issue.

specific.title: phoneme
specific.description:
The smallest unit of speech sound.

Examples include:

  • Cat has 3 phonemes: c/a/t
  • Truck has 4 phonemes: t/r/u/ck.

specific.title: phonic knowledge
specific.description: The ability to decode and encode words using knowledge of grapheme–phoneme relationships.

specific.title: phonological awareness
specific.description: The ability to hear, identify and say the separate parts of words (syllables, onsets, rimes and phonemes).

specific.title: phrase
specific.description: A group of related words that form part of a sentence and do not include both a verb and its subject.

specific.title: poetic forms
specific.description: Fixed forms within poetry that follow specific rules, such as ballad, sonnet, elegy, ode, dramatic monologue. The form will often be determined by the tone and subject matter. Note that some poets may deliberately subvert the fixed form.

specific.title: point of view
specific.description:
The position from which the information and events of a text are intended to be perceived by its audience. Point of view is constructed through the narrator, voice or images of the text and by characters or voices presented within it.

Point of view should not be confused with the term ‘perspective’ or with notions of opinion.

specific.title: polysyllabic words
specific.description: Words of 3 or more syllables.

specific.title: predict
specific.description: Suggest what may happen based on available information.

specific.title: prefix
specific.description: A bound morpheme made up of letters that appear before a base word to make a new word. For example, un- in ‘unhappy’ means ‘not’ (un + happy = not happy).

specific.title: preposition
specific.description: A word that is used before a noun, noun group or pronoun that connects it to another word in the sentence, e.g. in, on, after, before, by, under, over, of.

specific.title: prepositional phrase
specific.description:
A word or group of words that indicate a circumstance such as time, place, manner or causality.

See adjectival phrase and adverbial phrase

specific.title: prior knowledge
specific.description: The knowledge a person already has before encountering a particular topic.

specific.title: pronoun
specific.description: A word that is used in place of a noun. A pronoun may be personal (he, she, we, they), demonstrative (that, this) or relative (who).

specific.title: prosody
specific.description: Reading with expression using correct phrasing, intonation and attention to punctuation.

specific.title: pun
specific.description: A figure of speech where there is a play on words, usually created through the use of a homonym or homophone. Puns rely on more than one meaning of a word to emphasise the point.

specific.title: purpose
specific.description: To entertain, to inform or to persuade different audiences in different contexts. Composers use a number of ways to achieve these purposes: persuading through emotive language, analysis or factual recount; entertaining through description, imaginative writing or humour, and so on.

specific.title: question
specific.description: A sentence that seeks information by asking or requesting to elicit a response.

specific.title: question mark (?)
specific.description: A punctuation marker used at the end of a sentence to indicate that a question is being asked.

specific.title: questioning
specific.description: A reading comprehension strategy that may occur before, during, and/or after reading. The questions a reader may ask themselves can support their literal and/or inferential understanding of a text.

specific.title: quotation marks
specific.description: Punctuation markers used to indicate: quoted or direct speech; the actual words quoted from another source in formal writing; the titles of poems, songs, short stories or articles; or, to draw attention to an unusual or particular sense or usage of a word.

specific.title: quoted speech
specific.description: The exact words expressed by a person, reproduced in quotation marks. For example: ‘You'll never guess what I've just seen!’ exclaimed Loreta.

specific.title: reading
specific.description: To process written words, to derive and/or construct meaning. It is the product of word reading and language comprehension.

specific.title: recasting
specific.description: Recasting is a teaching strategy to support students in their oral language. A recast occurs when the teacher modifies a learner’s utterance by adding new or different grammar (syntax) or by using precise words.

specific.title: reciting
specific.description: Repeating a prepared text aloud, such as a published poem, to an audience. Reading should be prosodic and may occur from memory.

specific.title: recount
specific.description: Retell a series of events.

specific.title: reference
specific.description:
The use of a source of information in order to ascertain something.

The act of mentioning someone or something in speech or writing.

specific.title: reflection
specific.description: The thought process by which students develop an understanding and appreciation of their own learning. This process draws on both cognitive and affective experience.

specific.title: register
specific.description: The degree of formality or informality of language used for a particular purpose or in a particular social setting.

specific.title: regular plural word
specific.description: A noun comprising a free morpheme (base word) that is affixed to the inflected suffix, -s or -es, to indicate more than one.

specific.title: reported speech
specific.description:
Speech in a text used to communicate what someone else said, but without using the exact words. In reported speech the tense of the verbs is often changed.

For example:

  • She said that she was going to leave (indirect speech).
  • ‘I am going to leave', she said (direct speech).

specific.title: representation
specific.description: The way ideas are portrayed and represented in texts, using language devices, forms, features and structures of texts to create specific views about characters, events and ideas. Representation applies to all modes: spoken, written, visual and multimodal.

specific.title: responding
specific.description: The activity that occurs when students read, listen to or view texts. It encompasses the personal and intellectual connections a student makes with texts. It also recognises that students and the texts to which they respond reflect social contexts.

specific.title: return sweep
specific.description: The eye movement that takes the reader’s eyes from one end of the line of text to the start of the next line.

specific.title: rhetorical devices
specific.description: Strategies used by writers and speakers to achieve particular effects, such as, to stimulate the audience’s imagination or thought processes, to draw attention to a particular idea, or simply to display wit and ingenuity in composition.

specific.title: rhetorical question
specific.description: A question that is asked to provoke thought rather than require an answer.

specific.title: rhyme
specific.description: A repetition of similar speech sounds in 2 or more words, beginning from the last stressed vowel sound and carrying through any remaining syllables.

specific.title: rime
specific.description: The vowel and other speech sounds that occur at the end of a syllable. For example, the /-ig/ represents the rime in the word ‘big’.

specific.title: root
specific.description: A morpheme that gives the word its core meaning. A root may or may not stand alone as a word. Many roots in Standard Australian English derive from Latin and Greek.

specific.title: salience
specific.description:
A strategy used to highlight what is important in a text.

In an image, salience may be created through framing an object in the foreground, and/or by its size or distinct colour.

In written text, salience may be conveyed by positioning the most important idea at the beginning of a sentence, or through font styling such as the use of bold, underlined or italicised text.

specific.title: schwa
specific.description: A reduced vowel phoneme occurring in an unaccented (unstressed) syllable of a multisyllabic word. For example, in the word ‘problem’ the final vowel phoneme is unstressed and is said quickly and quietly, and with less emphasis.

specific.title: segment
specific.description: The act of separating a spoken word into its syllables and/or phonemes.

specific.title: sentence
specific.description:
A collection of words that conveys a complete thought, typically containing a subject and predicate. A sentence:

  • may express a statement, exclamation, command or question
  • comprises a main clause and sometimes one or more subordinate clauses
  • begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, exclamation mark or question mark.

See clause (main), simple sentence, compound sentence and complex sentence

specific.title: simile
specific.description:
A figure of speech that compares the similar qualities of 2 different things. The comparison usually includes like, as or as if.

See figurative language

specific.title: simple sentence
specific.description: A complete message that contains a subject and predicate, forming a single independent clause.

specific.title: single-letter grapheme
specific.description:
One letter used to represent one phoneme (speech sound).

See phoneme

specific.title: split digraph
specific.description:
Two graphemes that are split by a consonant to represent a long vowel phoneme.

For example:

  • a-e in cake
  • i-e in side
  • o-e in rope.

specific.title: spoken text
specific.description: Communication produced using spoken words and delivered either face-to-face or digitally.

specific.title: spoonerism
specific.description:
A language device, sometimes a slip of the tongue, by which corresponding phonemes or morphemes are switched between 2 words or within a word.

For example:

  • butterfly becomes flutterby
  • It's pouring with rain becomes it’s roaring with pain.

See word play

specific.title: Standard Australian English
specific.description: A system of standard English language, characterised by the perceived consistent usage of words and syntax across Australian political, business, media and education contexts. While it is always dynamic and evolving, it is recognised as the ‘common language’ of Australians.

specific.title: style
specific.description:
The way in which the effects of distinctive language forms and features of a text, often including those specific to its medium, combine to generate an overall impression.

Particular style elements may be observed in multiple works by the same author, from the same genre, or written during the same time period or artistic movement.

specific.title: subject
specific.description: The noun (or noun group) in a sentence that conveys who or what the clause is about.

specific.title: subject matter
specific.description: The topic or content of a text. For example, an information report on marine vessels may include content about construction materials, and different types of boats and engines.

specific.title: subjective language
specific.description: Words used to communicate based on opinion, feelings or personal biases.

specific.title: subject–verb agreement
specific.description: Occurs when the writer or speaker selects the correct verb for the noun or noun group to which it is referring. For example: The bike was here (not: The bike were here).

specific.title: subordinating conjunction
specific.description: A word or group of words that function to link a dependent clause to an independent clause.

specific.title: subvert
specific.description: To compose or respond to a text in ways that are different from the widely accepted reading or different from the conventional genre. For example, Roald Dahl's Revolting Rhymes provides a subverted reading of Cinderella. The purpose of producing a subverted reading of a text might be to entertain or to raise questions about the meaning or inherent values in the original text.

specific.title: suffix
specific.description:
A bound morpheme comprising a letter or group of letters that attach to a base word to make a new word.

For example:

  • The -s in dogs is an inflected suffix that marks plurality.
  • The derivational suffix, -ion can be added to the end of the verb, protect, to form the noun, protection.

See derivational word form and inflected word forms

specific.title: summarise
specific.description: Express, concisely, the relevant details.

specific.title: sustained reading
specific.description: Independently reading texts to expand and maintain comprehension.

specific.title: syllabification
specific.description: The process of segmenting a multisyllabic word into its syllables.

specific.title: syllable
specific.description: A unit of sound within a word that contains a vowel phoneme and feels like one ‘beat’. For example, a word with 3 syllables is: won-der-ful.

specific.title: symbol
specific.description: An object, character or entity that can be understood to represent a larger idea, action or feeling. Depending on context, audience and purpose, symbols can have commonly agreed or reinforced associations, or they can be dynamic. Symbols can operate within texts, or they can serve as meaning-making devices of language in the real world.

specific.title: synonym
specific.description: A word or phrase that has the same or a similar meaning to another word or phrase. For example, sick and ill.

specific.title: synthesise
specific.description: Put together various elements to make a whole.

specific.title: temporal connective
specific.description: A word or group of words that indicates when something is happening, e.g. first, next, finally, before, after, then.

specific.title: tense
specific.description:
The form of the verb that indicates when something is happening in relation to the speaker’s time: past, present or future.

For example:

  • I ate bananas (past).
  • I am eating bananas (present).
  • I will eat bananas (future).

specific.title: text
specific.description: Any written, spoken/signed, nonverbal, visual, auditory or multimodal communication. Texts may be extended unified works, a series of related pieces or a single, simple piece of communication.

specific.title: text features
specific.description: Structural or stylistic components that combine to construct meaning and achieve purpose. Can be recognisable as characterising particular types of texts.

specific.title: theme
specific.description: An overarching or recurring idea that describes attitudes or values that are perceived in a text. A theme may range from the understood ‘moral’ of a text to philosophical observations that the audience makes about the events, characters and experiences depicted in a text. A text may have more than one theme.

specific.title: Tier 1 words
specific.description: Basic-level, everyday words, e.g. dog, baby, happy, pretty, was, come, said.

specific.title: Tier 2 words
specific.description:
General academic words that can be used across a variety of domains. They are of high utility for mature language users and are commonly used in written language.

Tier 2 words add power and precision to written and spoken language, but many Tier 2 words are most commonly found in written language, e.g. contradict, precede, stale, awful, snuggle.

specific.title: Tier 3 words
specific.description: Words that are used rarely (low frequency) and only in highly specific situations, e.g. decibel, cataclysm, atom.

specific.title: tiered words
specific.description: Vocabulary classified according to complexity and use.

specific.title: topic sentence
specific.description: A sentence that usually occurs at the start of a paragraph and outlines the main idea of that paragraph.

specific.title: trigraph
specific.description:
Three letters used to represent one phoneme.

For example:

  • the tch in catch.
  • the igh in flight.

specific.title: upper/lower-case letters
specific.description:
Two visible forms of alphabetic letters. Lower-case letters are generally used, except when it is necessary to:

  • indicate specific names (proper nouns) such as those of people, organisations, titles or countries
  • indicate the beginning of a sentence or the initial letter of a proper noun
  • write headings
  • achieve a particular effect, such as to indicate shouting.

specific.title: verb
specific.description:
A word that tells what is happening. Different types of verbs include:

  • action verbs: They danced ...
  • thinking verbs: I forgot ...
  • feeling verbs: We like ...
  • saying verbs: He whispered ...
  • relating verbs: They are ....

specific.title: verb group
specific.description:
A group of words built around a verb.

Verb groups:

  • may include auxiliary verbs (‘helping’ verbs used to indicate tense or modality), e.g. I am going soon. I must leave before dark.
  • are sometimes referred to as a complex verb or compound verb.

specific.title: visual texts
specific.description: Texts that consist of or include images. Visual elements in texts may contribute to meaning. Visual design elements in a text may include choices of lines, symbols, vectors, size and colour.

specific.title: visualise
specific.description: A comprehension strategy used to create a mental image from a text read, viewed or heard. To visualise is to bring the text to life, engage the imagination, and use a person’s senses.

specific.title: voice
specific.description:
The way in which language is used and/or interpreted to represent particular thoughts, opinions or perspectives. This includes the authorial voice or the voice of a narrator, character or persona within a text.

Describes the relationship between the action expressed by the verb and the subject/object of the sentence. For example, ‘active voice’ is where the subject performs the action, ‘The cat broke the vase’; ‘passive voice' is where the object is acted upon, ‘The vase was broken by the cat’.

In speaking, a description of the oral production of text.

See point of view for ‘narrative voice’

specific.title: vowel
specific.description:
A sound that is voiced with the mouth open and not obstructed by the lips, teeth or tongue. For example: the short /o/ phoneme in the word ‘dog’.

Often represented by the graphemes: a, e, i, o, u.

specific.title: vowel digraph
specific.description:
Two vowel graphemes that represent one phoneme.

For example:

  • ea in cream
  • ai in snail
  • oo in chook.

specific.title: word association
specific.description: The relationship between a word and other words that are semantically related in a text.

specific.title: word play
specific.description:
Experimenting with and manipulating language.

See pun and spoonerism
